name: Apple cider vinegar toner

lead: People mix apple cider vinegar with water and apply it to the face as a toner, aiming at less oil, fewer breakouts and clearer skin.

ACV is about 5% acetic acid, and proponents believe the acidity balances or clears skin and cuts bacteria. No clinical studies on this use were found; Wikipedia describes the evidence for treating skin conditions with it as poor.

paras: It is diluted with water and applied with a cotton pad after cleansing, then rinsed or left on briefly depending on the person. It is usually part of a home-remedy skincare routine.
Burns from topical vinegar and eye injury on contact are documented, and acidity varies between brands. Major health organisations do not recommend it as a therapy.

angle.text: Diluted apple cider vinegar is applied as a toner in the hope that its acidity cuts oil and bacteria for clearer, less oily skin. The idea rests on its acetic acid content and anecdotes; no studies were found on its use for acne.

lead: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) toner is a diluted vinegar applied to the face after cleansing as a homemade toner. People use it in the hope of clearer, less oily skin with smaller-looking pores, and it is popular as a low-cost alternative to bottled astringents and acid toners.

ACV is made by fermenting apple juice and is about 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid, with malic acid contributing to the sour taste [1]. Unfiltered versions can contain the 'mother', a cellulose-rich biofilm of acetic acid bacteria [1]. Proponents describe the acidity as a way to bring skin toward a slightly acidic surface pH and to remove oil.

Wikipedia states that evidence for treating skin infections with vinegar is poor and that applying vinegar to skin conditions may cause burns [1]. Published dermatology research on topical ACV is limited to a few small studies in atopic dermatitis, in which dilute soaks did not improve skin barrier measures or change the skin bacterial microbiome [2].
infobox: Rose in the early 1800s; an 1810 cookbook has an apple cider vinegar recipe [1]

paras: Vinegar is about 94% water and 5% acetic acid, with malic acid from apples contributing to the sour taste; acidity can vary between brands [1].

Home-toner routines dilute ACV with water and apply it to the face with a cotton pad after washing, aiming at oil control, pore appearance and blemishes. Wikipedia does not describe skin-care routines, and its skin-related content concerns vinegar as a topical medication [1].
Topical application of vinegar for skin conditions is reported to be able to cause burns, and eye contact can cause irritation and sometimes corneal injury [1].

No studies of ACV toner for acne, oiliness or pores were found. A 2019 pilot split-arm study of 0.5 percent ACV soaks in atopic dermatitis reported no improvement in skin barrier integrity and noted that ACV's safety and efficacy are not well studied [2]. A 2021 study reported that dilute ACV soaks did not change the skin bacterial microbiome in atopic dermatitis [3]. Wikipedia reports a lack of high-quality clinical support for ACV health claims generally [1].
